What "no artificial sweeteners" actually means

Artificial sweeteners are the non-nutritive, synthetic sweeteners brand makers reach for when they want zero-sugar sweetness without giving up flavor. This guide screens every bar for four of them: sucralose, acesulfame potassium, aspartame, and saccharin.

18.6% of the bars in our database still have one on the label. Here is how often each one shows up, and where it usually hides.

Artificial sweeteners are not the same thing as sugar alcohols. Erythritol, maltitol, and xylitol are sugar alcohols, a different category with their own digestive tradeoffs, and they show up on a different screen entirely. If erythritol or maltitol is what you are actually trying to avoid, check our protein bars without sugar alcohols guide instead. Want both screens applied at once? Use the Bar Finder's Clean Ingredients filter, which excludes artificial sweeteners and sugar alcohols together.

Protein bars without sucralose

Sucralose, sold under the brand name Splenda, is the artificial sweetener actually driving this guide. It is a chlorinated sugar substitute, roughly 600 times sweeter than table sugar, with zero calories and no effect on blood sugar. People skip it for different reasons: reported digestive discomfort, an aftertaste they don't like, gut microbiome research they've read, or just a preference to avoid synthetic sweeteners entirely.

241 of the 1,298 bars we track, about 1 in 5, contain sucralose. We checked whether screening for sucralose on its own produces a different list than screening for all four artificial sweeteners this guide covers. It doesn't. Every bar in our database that contains acesulfame potassium, aspartame, or saccharin also contains sucralose, so protein bars without sucralose and protein bars without artificial sweeteners are the exact same 1,057 bars across 181 brands, already ranked in the full table below.

Here are 10 of the highest ingredient-quality sucralose-free bars to start with. The complete list, filterable by grade and searchable by brand, is further down this page.

See our protein bars without erythritol section, or the Clean Protein Bars guide, which requires an A or B ingredient grade with no artificial sweeteners or sugar alcohols at all. Net carbs matter more than the sweetener itself? Our Keto and Best Bars for Diabetics guides both allow sucralose, since it doesn't affect net carbs or blood sugar, but they exclude the maltitol family specifically.

What we found across our 1,000+ bar database

18.6%
of bars contain an artificial sweetener
241 bars, about 1 in 5 in our database, contain sucralose, acesulfame potassium, aspartame, or saccharin. Sucralose alone accounts for nearly all of it, showing up across low-sugar and high-fiber bars at every price point.
Sucralose shows up as a named ingredient, not always a trace amount.
Some of the 241 bars containing sucralose tuck it into a "contains 2% or less" catch-all clause near the end of the label. Others, including Anabar Monster Cookie Crunch and Anabar Fluff n' Butter, name it directly among the main ingredients.
Quest disqualifies completely.
All 16 tracked Quest flavors contain sucralose, part of how the brand hits its low-sugar, high-fiber macro targets across the entire lineup.
Barebells disqualifies completely too.
25 of 25 Barebells flavors contain sucralose, the same sweetener behind most of the disqualified bars on this list.
Whole-food bars dominate the qualifying pool.
KIND, Larabar, Bobo's, Aloha, and GoMacro all qualify at or near 100%. Their sweetness comes from dates, fruit, or honey rather than a manufactured sweetener.
A mixed lineup is common, not rare.
Wonderslim, think!, 1st Phorm, and Power Crunch are examples of brands that split meaningfully between qualifying and disqualified flavors within the same lineup.
181 brands still represented.
Even with 18.6% of the database disqualified, the qualifying pool spans a wide range of protein levels, price points, and ingredient grades.
Acesulfame potassium never shows up alone.
All 18 bars containing acesulfame potassium also contain sucralose. Neither David nor BalanceDiet, the only two brands using it, use it as a standalone sweetener.

Frequently asked questions

We screen for Sucralose, Acesulfame Potassium, Aspartame, and Saccharin. These are the non-nutritive artificial sweeteners that actually show up in protein bar ingredient lists. Any bar listing one of these gets flagged, regardless of how small the amount looks on the label.
No. Stevia leaf extract, Reb A, and monk fruit (luo han guo) extract are plant-derived sweeteners, not synthetic ones, so they don't count against a bar on this page. They show up constantly in the qualifying bars on this list. If you want to avoid all non-sugar sweeteners, including plant-derived ones, check the ingredient list yourself.
Yes, by a wide margin. Sucralose shows up in 241 bars, about 19% of our database. Acesulfame potassium is a distant second, and we found zero bars in the current database containing aspartame or saccharin.
Yes, across the entire lineup. All 16 tracked Quest flavors contain sucralose, part of how the brand hits its low-sugar, high-fiber numbers.
Yes. All 25 Barebells flavors contain sucralose, the same sweetener driving most of the artificial-sweetener bars on this list.
1,057 bars across 181 brands clear our artificial sweetener screen, led by whole-food brands like KIND, Larabar, and Bobo's that qualify at or near 100%. The full ranked list is in the table below, sorted by ingredient quality.
Not especially. It shows up in 18 bars, about 1.4% of our database, mostly concentrated in just two brands, David and BalanceDiet, almost always stacked alongside sucralose rather than used alone.
Yes, and it's common. NuGo splits mostly clean: 28 of 30 flavors qualify. Wonderslim splits the other way, with 20 of its 23 flavors landing on the disqualified side. think! splits closer to NuGo than to Wonderslim, with 19 of its 22 flavors qualifying.
Sucralose and acesulfame potassium add intense sweetness with zero sugar and negligible calories, which is why they show up so often in bars marketed as "low sugar," "keto friendly," or high-protein with a low calorie count. The tradeoff for some people is an artificial aftertaste or a personal preference to avoid non-nutritive sweeteners altogether.
No, they are two different categories. Artificial sweeteners are synthetic, calorie-free sweeteners like sucralose and acesulfame potassium, the four screened on this page. Sugar alcohols, like erythritol, maltitol, and xylitol, are a separate category with their own digestive tradeoffs and a different scoring screen. If erythritol or maltitol is what you actually want to avoid, see our protein bars without sugar alcohols guide, or use the Bar Finder's Clean Ingredients filter to screen out both at once.
Yes. 241 of the 1,298 bars we track, about 1 in 5, list sucralose on the ingredient label. It's the most common artificial sweetener in the category by a wide margin, see the breakdown above.
1,057 bars across 181 brands are sucralose-free. That's the exact same set as our full no-artificial-sweeteners list, since every bar in our database containing acesulfame potassium, aspartame, or saccharin also contains sucralose. See the sucralose-free picks above or the full ranked list below.
Barebells (25 of 25 flavors), Wonderslim (20 of 23), Pure Protein (18 of 18), FITCRUNCH (17 of 17), and Quest (16 of 16) lead the list, all using it to hit a low-sugar or high-fiber number across nearly their entire lineup.
